Assume AC as used to select the regression version. Fix a statistical experiment indexed by $\theta$, a point $x$, a real
regression target $m_\theta(x)$, and a real-valued estimator
$T_x$ of that target, meaning a measurable statistic with target space
$\mathbb R$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. At this point, use the
squared-error loss
$$L_x(\theta,a)=(a-m_\theta(x))^2,\qquad a\in\mathbb R.$$
Its **pointwise squared-error risk** is the possibly infinite quantity
$$R_x(\theta,T_x)=\int (T_x(z)-m_\theta(x))^2\,P_\theta(dz)\in[0,\infty].$$
This is the deterministic-rule specialization of the risk in
[[def-loss-function-and-risk]]: the action space is $\mathbb R$ with its
Borel sigma-algebra, the action is $T_x(z)$, and the loss section is
measurable because it is continuous in $a$. The integral is nonnegative, so
it is defined without a finite-moment assumption.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real random variables on a probability
space, with $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$, and choose a regular conditional law
$Q(x,dy)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$. On
$D=\{x:\int |y|\,Q(x,dy)<\infty\}$ define
$m(x)=\int y\,Q(x,dy)$, and put $m(x)=0$ off $D$. By
[[cor-conditional-expectation-as-a-measurable-function-of-the-conditioning-variable]],
$m$ is Borel measurable and $m(X)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E[Y\mid\sigma(X)]$. A **regression target** is the resulting
$P_X$-almost-sure equivalence class; a **chosen regression-function version**
is the particular Borel function selected by the specified conditional law.

Pointwise smoothness is an additional hypothesis on the chosen version. It is
not implied by existence of conditional expectation, and statements about
$m(x)$ at a specified point use that selected version.

derivations.claim: Write $T_x-m_\theta(x)=(T_x-\mathbb E_\theta T_x)+b_\theta(x)$. Squaring and taking expectations gives $\mathbb E_\theta[(T_x-m_\theta(x))^2]=\mathbb E_\theta[(T_x-\mathbb E_\theta T_x)^2]+b_\theta(x)^2$, because $\mathbb E_\theta[T_x-\mathbb E_\theta T_x]=0$.
By [F1] the left side of step 1.1 is the pointwise risk, and by [F2] its first term on the right is the variance. This is the asserted identity.

Thus $v(x-hu)=v(x)-huv'(x)+\tfrac12h^2u^2v''(x)+h^2u^2r_{v,h}(u)$. On compact kernel support the remainder tends uniformly to zero. Under the global alternative it is uniformly bounded and tends to zero for each fixed $u$: split the remainder integral at $|u|\le A$, use uniform continuity near $x$ on that fixed set, and bound the remaining part by $C\int_{|u|>A}u^2K(u)\,du\to0$ as $A\to\infty$. For the rapid-tail alternative put $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. For $v=f,mf$, $\int|v|<\infty$ and $h^{-1}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}K((x-z)/h)|v(z)|\,dz\le\epsilon_hh^2\delta^{-3}\int|v|=o(h^2)$. derivations.claim: Write $r_h(u)=m(x-hu)-m(x)+hu m'(x)$. Taylor's integral formula bounds $|r_h(u)|\le C h^2u^2$ and gives $r_h(u)/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)u^2$ pointwise. It also gives $|r_h(u)|\le C h|u|$ and $r_h(u)/(h|u|)\to0$ for each nonzero $u$. These bounds hold on compact kernel support for small $h$, or globally under the alternative assumptions. With $R_j=\int K(u)u^jf(x-hu)r_h(u)\,du$, splitting at a fixed $|u|\le A$ and controlling the tails by $\int_{|u|>A}u^2K(u)\,du$ proves $R_0=\tfrac12h^2m''(x)f(x)\mu_2+o(h^2)$ and $R_1=o(h)$. The same split yields $S_0\to f(x)$, $S_2\to f(x)\mu_2$; symmetry and the first-order expansion of $f$ give $S_1=-h f'(x)\mu_2+o(h)=O(h)$. For the rapid-tail alternative, write $z=x-hu$ and split at $|z-x|=\delta$. The far parts of $S_0,S_1,S_2$ are respectively $o(h^2),o(h),o(1)$, since $K((x-z)/h)\le\epsilon_hh^3/|x-z|^3$ and $\int f=1$. The far parts of $R_0,R_1$ are $o(h^2),o(h)$: expand $r=m(z)-m(x)-m'(x)(z-x)$ and use $\int |m|f<\infty$ with $|z-x|\ge\delta$. On the near region the preceding local bounds and the integrable $u^2K$ apply; letting $\delta\to0$ after $h\to0$ gives the same remainder limits. These estimates also make every stated integral finite.

The determinant tends to $f(x)^2\mu_2>0$. Since $T_j=m(x)S_j-hm'(x)S_{j+1}+R_j$ for $j=0,1$, the affine terms in the intercept cancel exactly and $m_{\mathrm{LL},h}(x)-m(x)=(S_2R_0-S_1R_1)/D_h$. Step 1.1 makes $S_1R_1=o(h^2)$ and gives the asserted coefficient after division by the positive limiting determinant.

derivations.claim: For the general assertion truncate $L$ to $L_A=L\mathbf1_{\{|u|\le A,\ |L(u)|\le A\}}$. The expectation of $(nh)^{-1}\sum_iL_A(U_i)$ is $\int L_A(u)f(x-hu)\,du\to f(x)\int L_A$ by uniform density convergence on its fixed compact support. Its variance is at most $(nh)^{-1}\int L_A(u)^2f(x-hu)\,du=O_A((nh)^{-1})\to0$. The elementary bound $\mathbb P(|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon)\le\operatorname{Var}(V)/\epsilon^2$ follows by integrating $\epsilon^2\mathbf1_{\{|V-\mathbb EV|>\epsilon\}}\le(V-\mathbb EV)^2$. Thus the truncated average converges in probability.

The expectation of the absolute difference between the full and truncated averages is at most $C\int|L-L_A|$, using the global density bound or its bound on the shrinking image of the compact support of $L$. This tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Markov's bound, obtained from $\epsilon\mathbf1_{\{Z>\epsilon\}}\le Z$ for $Z\ge0$, makes this difference uniformly small in probability. Also $\int L_A\to\int L$. First choosing $A$ large and then $n$ large proves the general assertion.

For the rapid-tail case and $L(u)=u^jK(u)$, $j=0,1,2$, restrict first to $|x-X_i|\le\delta$, where the density is bounded. The same truncation proof works there. The expected absolute contribution of the remaining observations is at most $\epsilon_h h^{2-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-3}f(z)\,dz\to0$, where $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$. Thus the same scalar limits hold for these three moments without a global density bound.

A zero determinant lies outside a fixed neighborhood of this positive limit, so its probability tends to zero.

The weighted response average has integrable absolute value, since it is bounded by $\sum_i|Y_i|\mathbf1_{\{Z_i>0\}}$. Conditioning on the predictors gives mean bias $\mathbb E[Q/T;T>0]+(a_0-m(x))\mathbb P(T=0)$. Change of variables gives $a\asymp h$, and [F3] gives $c=b/a=m_h(x)-m(x)=O(h^2)$. Bounded $m$ on the active region yields $|B_i|\le C Z_i$, $\mathbb EZ_i^2=O(h)$ and $\mathbb E(B_i-cZ_i)^2=O(h)$, by $R(K)<\infty$ and the appropriate density bound. Under the rapid-tail alternative, integrability follows instead from $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$. The bounds $\mathbb EZ_i^2=O(h)$ and $\mathbb E(B_i-cZ_i)^2=O(h)$ still hold: inside a fixed smooth neighborhood $m,f$ are bounded; outside it $K((x-z)/h)^2\le C h^6/|x-z|^6$ and $\int m^2f\le\mathbb E Y^2<\infty$. Positivity near zero implies there are $A,\kappa>0$ and a Borel set $J\subset[-A,A]$ of positive measure on which $K\ge\kappa$: the positive neighborhood is the countable union of its level sets $\{K\ge1/k\}$. Hence $p_h=\mathbb P((x-X_i)/h\in J)\asymp h$. The count $N$ is binomial. On $G=\{N\ge np_h/2\}$, $T\ge c_1h$. With $\gamma=1-e^{-1}-1/2>0$, Markov's bound applied to $e^{-N}$ gives $\mathbb P(G^c)\le e^{np_h/2}(1-p_h+p_he^{-1})^n\le e^{-\gamma np_h}\le e^{-c_2nh}$. In particular $T=0$ is contained in $G^c$.

On $G$, $R/T=R/a-R(T-a)/(aT)$. Since $\mathbb ER=0$, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds $|\mathbb E[R/a;G]|$ by $a^{-1}(\mathbb ER^2)^{1/2}\mathbb P(G^c)^{1/2}$. Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$,
a prediction point $x\in\mathbb R$, a bandwidth $h>0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$, and a fixed fallback
$a_0\in\mathbb R$. For data $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$, put
$$D_{n,h}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h).$$
The **Nadaraya–Watson estimator** of the pointwise target $m(x)$ is
$$\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h}(x)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n K((x-X_i)/h)Y_i}{D_{n,h}(x)},&D_{n,h}(x)>0,\\[6pt] a_0,&D_{n,h}(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
For fixed $x,h,n$, this is a statistic of the observed sample with real target
$m(x)$, in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The fallback is part
of the definition. Kernel regularity and bandwidth assumptions used for bias
or variance results are stated in those results.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic estimating the pointwise target
$m(x)$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case $p=1$ is the
**local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for a given
sample is implicit in this definition.

Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $M_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)\to f(x)\operatorname{diag}(1,\mu_2)$ in probability. Put $V_n=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)(1,U_i)^\mathsf T(1,U_i)$. The scalar generalization proved in [F3] applies also to a continuous multiplier $\sigma^2(x-hu)$: on fixed truncated support this multiplier converges uniformly to $\sigma^2(x)$ and is bounded, and the tail expectation is bounded by $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}|L|$. Thus, for $L=K^2$ the $(0,0)$ entry tends to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. In the rapid-tail alternative, local truncation remains valid. For $j=0,1,2$ the expected absolute far contribution to $V_{n,j}$ is bounded by $C h^{5-j}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}|z-x|^{j-6}\sigma^2(z)f(z)\,dz=o(1)$, since $\int\sigma^2f\le\mathbb EY^2$. Also $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ follows from boundedness and the rapid tail. For the local-linear conclusion, $\int(1+u^2)K^2<\infty$ permits $L=K^2u^j$, $j=0,1,2$, by the same truncation argument. All entries then converge to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)\int K^2u^{j+k}$; symmetry makes the off-diagonal limit zero. Terms with $K(U_i)=0$ are interpreted as zero. Every active response-law variance is finite almost surely; these are variances under the specified conditional response laws, without an assumption of unconditional square integrability.

On the event $\sum_iK(U_i)>0$, [F1], conditional response independence, and [F4] give $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat m_{\mathrm{NW},h_n}(x)\mid X_{1:n})=\dfrac{\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)}{(\sum_iK(U_i))^2}$. Writing $M_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)$ and $V_{n,00}=(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)^2\sigma^2(X_i)$ makes the scaled variance $V_{n,00}/M_{n,00}^2$, which converges to $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)/f(x)^2$. The zero-denominator event has probability tending to zero by [F3]'s $(0,0)$ entry, so the same convergence holds with the fallback.

On a nonsingular local-linear design matrix, weighted least squares gives conditional variance $(nh_n)^{-1}e_0^\mathsf TM_n^{-1}V_nM_n^{-1}e_0$, where $e_0=(1,0)^\mathsf T$. The limit matrix is diagonal with entries $f(x)$ and $f(x)\mu_2$, so its inverse has first diagonal entry $1/f(x)$; the $(0,0)$ limit of $V_n$ is $f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$. Matrix inversion is continuous at this invertible limit, because its entries are quotients of entries of the adjugate by the nonzero determinant. Thus the scaled conditional variance converges to $R(K)\sigma^2(x)/f(x)$. By [F3] the singular-design event has probability tending to zero, and the fallback does not change convergence in probability.

For the extra Nadaraya–Watson clause, choose $A,\kappa>0$ with $J=\{|u|\le A,K(u)\ge\kappa\}$ of positive measure, possible since $\int K=1$. Its predictor count is binomial with success probability $p_h\asymp h$. On $G_n=\{N\ge np_h/2\}$, $T_n=n^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)\ge c_1h$, whereas Markov's bound applied to $e^{-N}$ gives $\mathbb P(G_n^c)\le\exp(-c_2nh)$. The truncation argument of step 1.1 also proves $V_{n,00}\to f(x)\sigma^2(x)R(K)$ in $L^1$: the bounded truncated average converges in $L^2$, while the expected absolute tail is uniformly small. On $G_n$, $(T_n/h)^{-2}$ is bounded and converges in probability to $f(x)^{-2}$. It follows that the expectation of the scaled conditional variance on $G_n$ has the stated limit: separate $V_{n,00}$ into its constant limit and an $L^1$ error, and use bounded convergence in probability for the reciprocal factor. On $G_n^c$, the conditional variance is at most the active-region bound on $\sigma^2$, since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, or the fallback is deterministic. Hence its scaled expectation is $O(nh e^{-c_2nh})\to0$ in those alternatives. Under rapid tails, the conditional variance is at most $\sum_i\sigma^2(X_i)$; the count among the other $n-1$ observations is independent of $X_i$ and is below $np_h/2$ on $G_n^c$. Its binomial lower-tail bound gives $\mathbb E[\sigma^2(X_i);G_n^c]\le\mathbb EY^2 e^{-c_3nh}$. Thus the bad-event contribution is at most $n\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_3nh}$. For this rapid-tail unconditional clause assume also $nh^3\to\infty$; then $nh\ge n^{2/3}$ eventually and its scaled contribution vanishes.

Let $A_n$ be the response-law mean of the Nadaraya–Watson fit, including its fallback, and let $m_h=\int Kmf/\int Kf$. The kernel integrals and localization or global bounds imply $m_h\to m(x)$. Put $Z_i=K(U_i)$ and $R_n=n^{-1}\sum_i Z_i(m(X_i)-m_h)$. Then $\mathbb ER_n=0$ and $\mathbb ER_n^2\le n^{-1}\mathbb E[Z_1^2(m(X_1)-m_h)^2]=o(h/n)$: after change of variables, continuity at $x$ handles a fixed compact $u$-set and the integrable $K^2$ tail is dominated by bounded $f,m$. On $G_n$, $A_n-m_h=R_n/T_n$, so its expected square is $o((nh)^{-1})$. On $G_n^c$, $A_n$ and $m_h$ are bounded in the compact/global alternatives. Under rapid tails, the far part of the second-moment integral is $O(h^6)\int m^2f=o(h)$, and the leave-one-out binomial argument in step 3.1 gives $\mathbb E[A_n^2;G_n^c]\le n\mathbb EY^2e^{-c_4nh}+a_0^2\mathbb P(G_n^c)$. Its expected squared bad-event contribution is therefore negligible in all stated cases, and $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)\le\mathbb E(A_n-m_h)^2=o((nh)^{-1})$. Bounded active-region means and variances, or the bound $\widehat m^2\le\sum_iY_i^2+a_0^2$ under rapid tails, make the Nadaraya–Watson fit square-integrable. Expanding its centered square and integrating first under the response laws gives total variance equal to the expected conditional variance plus $\operatorname{Var}(A_n)$. Step 3.1 therefore proves the unconditional Nadaraya–Watson expansion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $h=h_n$. By [A2], the chosen regression function is $m(t)=0$ and the conditional response variance is $1$ at every $t$; the uniform design density is $1/2$ near $0$. The uniform kernel has $\mu_2=1/3$ and $R(K)=1/2$. For each $n\ge2$, the event $E_n=\{X_1\in[h/4,h/3],\ X_2=X_1+\delta\text{ for }0<\delta<h/12,\ |X_j|>h\text{ for }j\ge3\}$ has positive design density; on it exactly two kernel weights are positive. Since $X_1\ne X_2$, the two-column degree-one design matrix is invertible, so [F1] gives its intercept $(X_2Y_1-X_1Y_2)/(X_2-X_1)$.

Conditional on $E_n$, each sign pattern $(Y_1,Y_2)=(1,-1)$ and $(-1,1)$ has probability $1/4$, and the intercepts are respectively $(X_1+X_2)/\delta$ and $-(X_1+X_2)/\delta$. On the chosen $X_1$ interval, $X_1+X_2\ge h/2$, while the joint design density in $(X_1,\delta)$ is a positive constant. Integrating either signed tail therefore includes a positive multiple of $\int_0^{h/12}(h/2)\delta^{-1}\,d\delta=\infty$. Both positive and negative parts have infinite expectation, so the estimator has no Lebesgue expectation.

The bandwidth satisfies $h_n\to0$, $nh_n=n^{3/4}\to\infty$, and $nh_n^3=n^{1/4}\to\infty$, and the matrix is nonsingular on $E_n$. Thus the counterexample satisfies these local smoothness, kernel and bandwidth hypotheses while the finite-sample expectation does not exist; the singular-matrix fallback is not used on these samples.

Let $X$ have Lebesgue density $f$, with $f(x)>0$ at a fixed interior point
$x$, and let $f,m$ be $C^2$ near $x$. Let $K$ be a finite-valued Borel,
nonnegative, symmetric kernel with $\int K=1$,
$0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$ and $\int K^2<\infty$.

two derivatives are bounded and continuous on $\mathbb R$. In these first two alternatives, no continuity
or boundedness of $K$ is required. The global alternative supplies tail
control for noncompact kernels; local smoothness alone does not supply it.

to $\mu$** is the measure

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC as in [[def-regression-target-version]]. Fix $n\ge1$, a point
$x\in\mathbb R$, bandwidth $h>0$, degree $p\in\mathbb N_0$, a finite-valued
nonnegative Borel function $K$, and fallback $a_0\in\mathbb R$. Set
$u_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $r_p(u)=(1,u,\ldots,u^p)^\mathsf T$, let $Z$ be the matrix
whose $i$th row is $r_p(u_i)^\mathsf T$, let
$W=\operatorname{diag}(K(u_1),\ldots,K(u_n))$, and put
$M=Z^\mathsf TWZ$. If $M$ is nonsingular, define
$$\widehat\beta=M^{-1}Z^\mathsf TW(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)^\mathsf T,\qquad \widehat m_{p,h}(x)=\widehat\beta_0.$$
If $M$ is singular, define $\widehat m_{p,h}(x)=a_0$. For fixed $x,h,n,p$
and Borel $K$, this is a real statistic estimating the pointwise target
$m(x)$ as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. The case $p=1$ is the
**local-linear estimator**. No claim that $M$ is nonsingular for a given
sample is implicit in this definition.

Let $X_i$ be iid real random variables with density $f$ continuous and
positive at a fixed point $x$. Let $K$ be finite-valued Borel, nonnegative,
symmetric, with $\int K=1$ and $0<\mu_2=\int u^2K(u)\,du<\infty$.
Assume compact kernel support, a globally bounded density $f$, or a bounded
rapid-tail kernel satisfying $\sup_{|u|\ge A}|u|^3K(u)\to0$.
For $h=h_n\to0$ with $nh_n\to\infty$, set $U_i=(x-X_i)/h_n$ and
$$M_n=\frac1{nh_n}\sum_{i=1}^nK(U_i)\begin{pmatrix}1\\U_i\end{pmatrix}(1,U_i).$$
Then
$$M_n\longrightarrow f(x)\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\mu_2\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{in probability},$$
and $\mathbb P(M_n\text{ is nonsingular})\to1$.
More generally, the proof establishes $(nh_n)^{-1}\sum_i L(U_i)\to f(x)\int L$
for any integrable Borel function $L$, if $f$ is bounded globally or $L$
has compact support. Boundedness or square integrability of $L$ is unnecessary.

derivations.claim: Put $h=h_n$, $U_i=(x-X_i)/h$, $S_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^j$ and $r_h(u)=m(x-hu)-m(x)+hu m'(x)$. Then $S_0\to f(x)$, $S_2\to f(x)\mu_2$ by [F2]. Symmetry and the first-order density expansion give $\mathbb ES_1=-hf'(x)\mu_2+o(h)$; the tail is controlled by $u^2K$ under the global alternative. Also $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)\le C(nh)^{-1}\int u^2K^2$, using localization or the global density bound. In the rapid-tail alternative its local part has this bound, and the far contribution to $\operatorname{Var}(S_1)$ is at most $C h^2n^{-1}\int_{|z-x|>\delta}f(z)|z-x|^{-4}\,dz$, hence no larger than $O((nh)^{-1})$. Since $nh^3\to\infty$, $(S_1-\mathbb ES_1)/h\to0$ in probability by the variance bound, so $S_1=O_P(h)$.

Set $R_j=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK(U_i)U_i^jr_h(U_i)$. Taylor's integral formula gives $|r_h(u)|\le Ch^2u^2$ and $r_h(u)/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)u^2$. The truncation proof of [F2] applies to this varying integrand: on any fixed set where $|u|$ and $K(u)$ are bounded it converges uniformly, its average has variance $O_A((nh)^{-1})$, and the absolute tail expectation is at most $C\int_{\mathrm{tail}}u^2K$. Hence $R_0/h^2\to\tfrac12m''(x)f(x)\mu_2$ in probability. Furthermore $|r_h(u)|\le Ch|u|$ and $r_h(u)/(h|u|)\to0$ pointwise. Splitting the integral as before gives $\mathbb E|R_1|/h\le\int K(u)|u||r_h(u)|f(x-hu)/h\,du\to0$. Markov's bound yields $R_1=o_P(h)$. Under the rapid-tail alternative these arguments are first applied on $|X_i-x|\le\delta$. For the far part put $\epsilon_h=\sup_{|u|\ge\delta/h}|u|^3K(u)\to0$ and expand $r=m(z)-m(x)-m'(x)(z-x)$. Its expected absolute contributions to $R_0/h^2$ and $R_1/h$ are bounded by $C_\delta\epsilon_h\int(1+|m|)f\to0$. The same tail estimate gives the stated expectation expansion for $S_1$. Thus all limits hold without global smoothness.

On a nonsingular design, [F1] and [F3] give $b_n-m(x)=(S_2R_0-S_1R_1)/(S_0S_2-S_1^2)$, since the constant and slope terms cancel exactly in the intercept. Steps 1.1–2.1 give $S_1R_1=o_P(h^2)$, and the denominator tends to $f(x)^2\mu_2>0$. Division gives the claimed coefficient. The singular-design event has probability tending to zero by [F2]; even after scaling by $h^{-2}$ the probability of any nonzero fallback contribution is at most that event probability, so it does not change convergence in probability. This argument integrates the response law separately for each design and never interchanges an undefined unconditional signed expectation.
